764.title: The kingdom splits (1 Kings 12)
764.hook: Rehoboam ignores the elders' counsel, and ten tribes leave
764.howItsDone: Jews read the division of the kingdom in the book of Kings; from here the story follows two kingdoms, Israel in the north and Judah, where David's house reigns.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Solomon's heart, no longer shalem, turned slowly. Your line was one small choice at a time. A new week begins, and his son faces his first test.

A new king, a crowd, and a request. Solomon has died. His son Rehoboam goes to Shechem, where all Israel has come to make him king. Their spokesmen don't waste words: your father made our yoke heavy. Lighten the hard service and the heavy yoke, and we will serve you. Rehoboam says, go away for three days, then come back. In those three days, he asks two groups for advice.
screen: `A CROWD AT SHECHEM.` → `LIGHTEN OUR YOKE.` → `COME BACK IN THREE DAYS.`

segments.voice: First he goes to the old men, in Hebrew the zekenim, the elders who had stood before his father Solomon. Their advice, in the 1917 Jewish translation: "If thou wilt be a servant unto this people this day, and wilt serve them, and answer them, and speak good words to them, then they will be thy servants for ever." Then he goes to the young men who grew up with him. They say the opposite. Tell them, my little finger is thicker than my father's loins. My father chastised you with whips; I will chastise you with scorpions. Rehoboam goes with the young men. On the third day he gives the people the hard answer, and they cry back: "to your tents, O Israel; now see to thine own house, David." The northern tribes walk away and make another man their king; only Judah stays with the house of David. A prophet had already spoken of ten tribes torn away; now it happens. Look at what the elders actually said. Not be weak. Not give in on everything. Be a servant this day: one day of humility, for a lifetime of loyalty. They had stood before Solomon and knew his reign from the inside. In this story the old counsel doesn't win because it's old. It carries weight because it came from people who had seen a reign from start to finish. Rehoboam had that advice in his hands, and he chose the voices that sounded like his own.

segments.voice: Let the face of someone who has been at something longer than you come clearly to mind, a grandparent, a mentor, a neighbor. What advice have they given you that you brushed aside, or what question could you ask them that you haven't yet? If you pray, you can ask to know good counsel when it comes.

765.title: The ravens (1 Kings 17:1–6)
765.hook: in drought, ravens bring Elijah bread and meat
765.howItsDone: Jews read Elijah's story in the book of Kings, and Elijah appears in Jewish practice beyond it, as in the cup of Elijah set out at the Passover seder.

segments.voice: Yesterday the kingdom split after Rehoboam set aside the zekenim. Your line was heed the old counsel. Today a prophet walks onto the stage with almost no introduction.

No family tree. No birth story. No call scene. Just a name and a place: Elijah the Tishbite, of the settlers of Gilead. He stands before King Ahab and says there will be no dew or rain in these years, except by his word. Then he leaves. God sends him to hide by a brook near the Jordan, in a land about to go dry. And the food that keeps him alive there comes from a source nobody would have picked.
screen: `ELIJAH THE TISHBITE.` → `NO DEW OR RAIN.` → `HIDE BY THE BROOK.`

segments.voice: God tells Elijah to hide by the brook Cherith. In the 1917 Jewish translation: "thou shalt drink of the brook; and I have commanded the ravens to feed thee there." And they do. "And the ravens brought him bread and flesh in the morning, and bread and flesh in the evening; and he drank of the brook." The Hebrew word is orvim, ravens. Of all birds. In the Torah's list of birds Israel may not eat, the raven is there by name, and here it is carrying bread and meat to a prophet, morning and evening, in a drought. Some later commentators wondered whether orvim might mean people instead of birds. The plain story keeps the birds, and keeps the strangeness: help arrives on the wings of something the Torah set apart as unfit for the table. There's a quieter point too. Elijah has just spoken a drought into the land, and the very next thing the text shows is that he has to be fed. He sits by a brook, waits, and accepts food from birds. After his big word, the prophet's next scene is about receiving. And it doesn't last: after a while, the text says, the brook dried up, because there had been no rain, and he'll have to move on. But for a time the help came, twice a day, from the last place he'd have looked.
screen: `HIDE BY THE BROOK CHERITH.` · `ORVIM: RAVENS, ON THE TORAH'S LIST.` · `THE PROPHET HAS TO BE FED.` · `THE BROOK DRIES UP.` · then, large: `THE RAVENS BROUGHT HIM BREAD AND FLESH.`

segments.voice: Remember a time someone helped you whom you didn't expect, a stranger, someone you had written off, someone you'd kept at arm's length, and let that face stay a moment. Then ask whether help is being offered today that you're refusing because of where it comes from. If you pray, you can give thanks for the ravens in your life.

766.title: The widow's jar (1 Kings 17:8–16)
766.hook: a widow shares her last flour, and the jar never runs out
766.howItsDone: Jews read the story of the widow of Zarephath in the book of Kings, where it is followed in the same chapter by Elijah's prayer for her son.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ravens brought Elijah his food by the brook. Your line was the ravens fed him. Today the brook is dry, and the help comes from someone with almost nothing.

At the gate of a town called Zarephath, a woman is gathering sticks. Not many. Just enough for one small fire. A stranger, dusty from the road, calls out to her: bring me a little water in a vessel, so I can drink. She turns to get it. Then he calls after her: and bring me, please, a piece of bread. She stops. Her answer is blunt, and it tells you everything about her kitchen.
screen: `THE GATE OF ZAREPHATH.` → `A LITTLE WATER, PLEASE.` → `AND A PIECE OF BREAD.`

segments.voice: Zarephath belongs to Zidon, outside the land of Israel. She answers Elijah with an oath, as the LORD your God lives, and then the plain truth: nothing baked, only a handful of meal in a jar and a little oil in a cruse. She's gathering sticks to make one last meal for herself and her son, so they can eat it and die. The Hebrew word for her jar is kad. Elijah says: don't be afraid. Go and do as you said, but make me a little cake first, and after that make some for yourself and your son. For the LORD has said the jar of meal won't be used up and the cruse of oil won't fail until the day the LORD sends rain. Hear what he's asking. Her last flour. To a stranger. Before her own child. And she does it. She, and he, and her house ate for many days, and in the 1917 Jewish translation: "The jar of meal was not spent, neither did the cruse of oil fail, according to the word of the LORD." Each day she reaches into a jar that should be empty, and there's enough for that day. Not a mountain of flour. Enough. Notice who this miracle runs through: not a king, not a priest, but a widow in a town of Zidon, at the end of her supplies, who shares first. Ravens fed Elijah; now a woman with nothing to spare feeds him. Giving, in this story, doesn't start with plenty. It starts with a handful.

segments.voice: Name what feels scarce for you right now, time, money, energy, patience, honestly, the way the widow did at the gate. Then think of one small thing you could still share from it, not from the surplus but from the handful, and let that thought settle. If you pray, you can ask for some of her courage.

767.title: Between two opinions (1 Kings 18:21–39)
767.hook: "How long halt ye between two opinions?" on Mount Carmel
767.howItsDone: Jews read the contest on Mount Carmel as a haftarah, and at the close of Yom Kippur the congregation calls out the people's words from this chapter, that the Lord is God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a widow's kad, her jar, didn't fail. Your line was the jar didn't fail. Today Elijah climbs a mountain to face a whole people.

Mount Carmel, and the slope is full of people. King Ahab has sent for all the children of Israel, and they've come up to watch a contest. On one side stand the prophets of Baal, the god Queen Jezebel favors. On the other stands one man: Elijah. The land has had no rain for a long time. Before any fire is lit, before any altar is built, Elijah turns, not to the king and not to the prophets, but to the people watching. And he asks them a question.
screen: `ALL ISRAEL ON MOUNT CARMEL.` → `ONE MAN AND A CROWD.` → `A QUESTION FOR THE PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: In the King James words: "How long halt ye between two opinions?" To halt, in old English, is to limp: someone hobbling, one foot on each side of a fork in the road, never quite walking down either. Then Elijah finishes the thought: if the Lord be God, follow him; but if Baal, then follow him. The text gives the crowd's reply. The people answered him not a word. Nobody wants to choose. Then the contest. Two altars, two bulls, no fire; whoever answers with fire is God. The prophets of Baal call out from morning until noon, and there was no voice, nor any that answered. Elijah rebuilds a broken altar of the Lord, has water poured over it until the trench runs full, and prays a short prayer. Fire falls and consumes everything, even the water in the trench. And the people who said not a word fall on their faces: "The LORD, he is the God; the LORD, he is the God." But the question came before the fire. Elijah was after an end to the limping. In Jewish practice, the people's cry from this chapter returns at the very end of Yom Kippur, called out by the whole congregation as the gates of the day close. A people that once could not answer at all now answers together. The story keeps the uncomfortable middle part, too: the long silence, the people waiting to see who would win before they spoke. It doesn't pretend that choosing is easy. It only asks how long.
screen: `HOW LONG HALT YE?` · `THE PEOPLE ANSWERED NOT A WORD.` · then, large: `FIRE ON THE REBUILT ALTAR.` · then: `THE LORD, HE IS THE GOD.`

segments.voice: Find the thing you've been limping on, one foot on each side: a call you keep almost making, a habit you keep almost dropping, a yes or a no left hanging, and notice what the waiting has cost. Then, quietly, let one side land, without acting on it yet, the way the people's silence finally turned into words. If you pray, you can ask for clarity.

768.title: Arise and eat (1 Kings 19:1–8)
768.hook: exhausted Elijah wants to die; an angel brings food and says "Arise and eat"
768.howItsDone: Jews read Elijah's flight to the wilderness as part of the book of Kings, and it is read in synagogue as a haftarah; the scene is often remembered as a picture of care for someone at the end of their strength.

segments.voice: Yesterday, on Carmel, Elijah asked a silent crowd how long they would halt between two opinions. Today, soon after the fire, the same prophet is running for his life.

A message arrives from the palace. Queen Jezebel has heard what happened on Carmel, and she sends Elijah a promise: by this time tomorrow, you'll be dead. The man who stood alone against a mountain full of prophets doesn't stand this time. He runs, south, out of the kingdom, to Beer-sheba. He leaves his servant there and keeps going, alone, a day's journey into the wilderness. He sits down under a broom tree, a scrubby desert bush. And the prophet who faced down a whole mountain says he's done.
screen: `A THREAT FROM THE QUEEN.` → `A DAY INTO THE WILDERNESS.` → `UNDER A BROOM TREE.`

segments.voice: His words are blunt. It is enough. Now, O Lord, take away my life, for I am not better than my fathers. Then he lies down and falls asleep. Notice the timing. This isn't Elijah after a failure. It's Elijah right after Carmel: fire fell from heaven at his word, and now he's under a bush asking to die. The text doesn't scold him for it, or call him weak or faithless. An angel touches him and says: "Arise and eat." By his head is a cake baked on hot stones and a jar of water. He eats, he drinks, and he lies back down. No lecture. Then the angel comes a second time, touches him again, and says it again: arise and eat, because the journey is too great for you. He gets up, eats, drinks, and in the strength of that food, the text says, he walks forty days and forty nights to Horeb, the mountain of God. Look at the order. Before anyone talks to Elijah about his calling, his fear or his future, someone feeds him and lets him sleep. Twice. Some readers notice how tender this scene is: the God who sent fire on Carmel sends a meal under a bush. The great conversation is still coming, on the mountain. But first, the body. A tired person can't hear much of anything, so the first word from heaven is the plainest one possible. Get up. Eat something.
screen: `IT IS ENOUGH.` · `A CAKE AND A JAR OF WATER.` · then, large: `ARISE AND EAT.` · then: `THE JOURNEY IS TOO GREAT FOR THEE.`

segments.voice: Ask your body a plain question, when did I last eat, drink water, or rest, and let your shoulders drop and your jaw loosen with a long breath out. If something heavy is pressing on you, set it beside you for now, the way Elijah's journey waited while he slept. And if a heaviness like his under the tree is ever yours, please reach out: in the US you can call or text 988, or call local emergency help.
Broom tree. Where an exhausted Elijah collapsed and asked to die, before an angel told him to eat. Today's word.

769.title: A still small voice (1 Kings 19:11–13)
769.hook: not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, but "a still small voice"
769.howItsDone: Jews read Elijah at Horeb as part of the book of Kings and as a haftarah, and the phrase kol demamah dakah appears in the Unetaneh Tokef prayer of the High Holy Days.

segments.voice: Yesterday, under the broom tree, an angel's first word was bread. Your line was but first, the body. Today, fed and rested, Elijah reaches the mountain.

What doest thou here, Elijah? The question comes to him in a cave on Horeb, the mountain of God, where he has spent the night after a long walk. He has an answer ready. I have been very jealous for the Lord. The people have torn down your altars and killed your prophets, and I, even I only, am left, and they want my life too. It's the answer of someone who believes he is the last one left. And instead of an argument, he's told: go out, and stand on the mountain.
screen: `A CAVE ON HOREB.` → `WHAT DOEST THOU HERE, ELIJAH?` → `GO OUT AND STAND.`

segments.voice: What happens next is told in a careful rhythm. A great and strong wind tears at the mountains and breaks the rocks in pieces. "But the LORD was not in the wind." After the wind, an earthquake; the Lord was not in the earthquake. After the earthquake, a fire; the Lord was not in the fire. Three times the noise builds, and three times: not there. And then, in the King James and the Jewish Publication Society words alike, "a still small voice." Elijah hears it, wraps his face in his cloak, and steps to the mouth of the cave. This is the prophet of Carmel, the man of fire. Fire fell at his word. And now he's shown that God is not in the fire. The Hebrew phrase, kol demamah dakah, is hard to translate, and readers have heard it different ways: a still small voice, a quiet whisper, even a sound of thin silence. The text doesn't settle it. Whatever it was, it was quiet enough to miss if you were waiting for thunder. One more detail, an honest one. The voice asks the very same question again, what doest thou here, Elijah, and Elijah gives the very same answer, word for word. The quiet doesn't magically fix him. But in that quiet he receives his next instructions, and learns he is not as alone as he thought. The wind really did break rocks. It just wasn't where God was speaking.
screen: `NOT IN THE WIND.` · `NOT IN THE EARTHQUAKE, NOT IN THE FIRE.` · then, large: `A STILL SMALL VOICE.` · then: `THE SAME QUESTION, ASKED AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Put the phone out of reach, and first notice the loud things, traffic, a fan, the noise in your own head, naming each one and letting it pass the way the wind, the earthquake and the fire passed. Then listen underneath, to your breath, the room itself, a quiet you usually talk over, staying at the mouth of the cave without waiting for anything to happen.
Demamah. The Hebrew for stillness, inside the phrase Elijah heard after the wind, the earthquake and the fire. Today's word.
Your line: quiet enough to miss. The noise was real; the voice was somewhere else. See you tomorrow.

770.title: Naboth's vineyard (1 Kings 21)
770.hook: the king takes a man's land through false witnesses; Elijah confronts him
770.howItsDone: Jews read Naboth's vineyard as part of the book of Kings, and the story is remembered as a picture of a powerful ruler abusing the courts to take what belonged to an ordinary family.

segments.voice: Yesterday, on Horeb, God was not in the wind or the fire but in something quiet enough to miss. Today that prophet goes back to the king, and he is anything but quiet.

A vineyard in Jezreel, beside the king's palace. It belongs to a man named Naboth. King Ahab wants it for a vegetable garden, and he offers what sounds fair: a better vineyard somewhere else, or its worth in money. Naboth says no, in the King James words: "The LORD forbid it me, that I should give the inheritance of my fathers unto thee." In Israel's law, family land was an inheritance, meant to stay with the family. Ahab goes home, lies on his bed, turns his face to the wall, and won't eat.
screen: `A VINEYARD BY THE PALACE.` → `THE INHERITANCE OF MY FATHERS.` → `A KING SULKING ON HIS BED.`

segments.voice: Queen Jezebel finds him there. Are you the king of Israel or not? Get up and eat. I'll get you the vineyard. She does it with paperwork: letters in Ahab's name, sealed with his seal, sent to the elders of Naboth's town. Call a fast. Seat Naboth at the head of the people. Set two worthless men opposite him to testify that he cursed God and the king. The elders do exactly what the letters say. Naboth is taken outside the city and stoned, and word comes back: Naboth is dead. Ahab goes down to take his vineyard. Notice how legal it all looks: a public fast, witnesses, a trial, a sentence. Only the truth is missing. And notice how many went along, the elders, the nobles, the witnesses; the text records no one in the town saying no. Then, as Ahab walks into his new vineyard, Elijah is waiting, sent by God with one question: "Hast thou killed, and also taken possession?" Ahab's reply: "Hast thou found me, O mine enemy?" To him, the man naming the wrong is the enemy. The story doesn't end in neat justice that afternoon; Ahab humbles himself, and the punishment is delayed. But the question has been asked out loud, to the king's face. This week brought a kingdom split, ravens, a widow's jar, fire on Carmel, bread under a broom tree, and a still small voice. Today the prophet's job is simplest of all: to speak for one man nobody else would speak for.
screen: `LETTERS IN THE KING'S NAME.` · `TWO FALSE WITNESSES.` · then, large: `HAST THOU KILLED, AND TAKEN?` · then: `O MINE ENEMY.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who was treated unfairly, a coworker blamed for someone else's mistake, a neighbor talked about behind their back, and notice who went along with it, maybe including you. Then hold in mind one small, real thing that could help: a true word to the right person, a message of support, a refusal to repeat the story.
Naboth's vineyard. The family land a king wanted, taken through letters, false witnesses and a death, until a prophet named it. Today's word.
Your line: hast thou killed, and taken. A wrong dressed up as proper is still a wrong. That's day seven hundred seventy.

trapdoor: what you thought: a king grabbing a garden.
what it means: a crime dressed up as law, and a prophet who names it plainly.
what a scholar hears: Naboth guards his nachalah, his inheritance; Elijah's verb, yarashta, is the verb for taking an heir's possession.

chat.says: Naboth got a trial, didn't he? So why does Elijah call it killing?
options: The trial was rigged with false witnesses; it looked legal, but the truth was missing.
Because Ahab himself threw the first stone at Naboth outside the city.
Because the trial was fair, but the punishment was far too harsh for it.
chat.meaning: Jezebel's letters set up a fast, a trial and two worthless witnesses. Every step had a form; only the truth was missing.

Jezreel.meaning: the town where Naboth's vineyard stood beside the palace

Jezebel.meaning: King Ahab's queen, who wrote the letters
